Accrual accounting records income when it’s earned and expenses when they’re incurred — even if you haven’t been paid or haven’t paid yet. Cash-basis accounting records income and expenses only when cash actually arrives or leaves your bank account. ([linkedin.com](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/investopedia-ulc_accrual-accounting-vs-cash-basis-accounting-activity-7314044326479552513-UDET?utm_source=openai))

Practically, accrual gives a clearer picture of activity for a period (showing what work was done and what’s owed), while cash-basis is simpler and shows actual cash flow. Because accrual matches revenues with the costs to earn them, banks and larger businesses often prefer it. The IRS also has rules: some businesses (for example, those with inventory or larger receipts) must use accrual methods for tax reporting. ([openstax.org](https://openstax.org/books/principles-finance-2e/pages/4-1-cash-versus-accrual-accounting?utm_source=openai))

If you want a short rule of thumb: cash = when money moves; accrual = when the work or obligation happens.
